Both research threads are complete. Here's the synthesis.

---

# THREAD A — DX Core 4, the DXI, and DX's stance on individual measurement

## A1. The framework: exact definitions and headline metrics

**Source of record:** Abi Noda, "Introducing the DX Core 4," *Engineering Enablement*, **Dec 10, 2024** — https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/introducing-the-dx-core-4 (also https://getdx.com/news/introducing-the-dx-core-4/ and the whitepaper landing at https://getdx.com/research/measuring-developer-productivity-with-the-dx-core-4/)

**Authorship and provenance, in Noda's own words:**
> "Laura Tacho (DX CTO) and I got to work on developing something new: a framework that encapsulates DORA, SPACE, and DevEx while providing a prescriptive approach. We involved Nicole, Michaela, Tom Zimmerman, and numerous experts and DX customers who helped us iterate on this framework over the course of several months."

Note the exact cast: **Nicole Forsgren, Michaela Greiler, Thomas Zimmermann**. Margaret-Anne (Peggy) Storey is named as a co-author of the *DevEx* framework and appears later as a commenter on Core 4's naming — she is credited in the lineage, not listed among the Core 4 iterators in this passage. Worth being precise about, since the framing "with Forsgren and Storey involved" is roughly right but not exactly what the primary source says.

**The origin story (useful, quotable):**
> "This came to a head for me personally after multiple conversations where executives asked me, 'So what exactly should we be measuring?' and my answer was, 'It depends.' These leaders wanted something more prescriptive, and we didn't have a good answer for them." — Abi Noda

**Why not just DORA/SPACE/DevEx (verbatim):**
> "**DORA** offers prescriptive metrics but has limited scope and usefulness due to focus on system performance. **SPACE** provides a framework for defining your own metrics, which is difficult to actually do. **DevEx** focuses on developer experience and self-reported metrics, but it is isolated from the broader concept of productivity."

### The four dimensions, verbatim

| Dimension | Primary metric | Noda's definition (verbatim) |
|---|---|---|
| **Speed** | Diffs per Engineer (or PRs per Engineer) | "provides a snapshot of the flow of work through the system" |
| **Effectiveness** | Developer Experience Index (DXI) | "measures key performance drivers that drive engineering speed and quality… an aggregated score from 14 standardized Likert-scale survey items, measuring a wide range of areas such as code quality, focus time, and CI/CD" |
| **Quality** | Change Failure Rate | "measuring how often changes deployed to production result in failures. CFR ensures that a focus on speed does not come at the cost of stability or reliability" |
| **Impact** | Percentage of Time Spent on New Capabilities | "reflects how much engineering effort is focused on building new features versus maintenance or KLTO work. A low percentage here might indicate teams are bogged down by inefficiencies or legacy systems" |

On naming: the newsletter calls the fourth dimension **"Impact"**; the docs and marketing frequently say **"Business Impact."** Both are DX's own usage — use whichever, but don't treat them as different things.

**Secondary metrics** (12 total, per the whitepaper): lead time, deployment frequency, perceived rate of delivery, time to 10th PR; ease of delivery, regrettable attrition (org level); failed deployment recovery time, perceived software quality, operational health/security; initiative progress and ROI, revenue per engineer (org level), R&D as % of revenue (org level).

**Product-side implementation names** (https://docs.getdx.com/dx-core-4/): Speed = "Pace of code integration" → PR throughput; Effectiveness = "Developer experience & friction" → DXI (survey only); Quality = "Reliability of changes" → change fail % or defect ratio; Impact = "Mix of work toward new capability" → innovation ratio.

**Claimed outcomes across 300+ orgs:** "3%–12% overall increase in engineering efficiency," "14% increase in R&D time spent on feature development," "15% improvement in employee engagement scores."

**Published benchmarks** (500+ companies, https://getdx.com/research/benchmarks/): Diffs/engineer/week — P50 **3.8**, P75 **4.67**, P90 **5.53**. DXI — P50 **76**, P75 **83**. Change failure % — P50 **3.46%**, P75 **3.05%**. Innovation ratio — P50 **61.72%**, P75 **65.06%**.

## A2. The DXI and the ROI claim

**Primary source:** "Developer Experience Index: The One Number You Need to Increase ROI per Engineer" — https://getdx.com/research/the-one-number-you-need-to-increase-roi-per-engineer/ (guide version: https://getdx.com/blog/guide-to-developer-experience-index/)

**The exact ROI line, twice in the same document:**
> "Each one-point gain in DXI score translates to saving **13 minutes per week per developer, equivalent to 10 hours annually**."
> "Most notably, DXI scores strongly correlate with time loss… The DXI is thus **the first validated measure of developer productivity that can be directly linked to dollars**."

**⚠️ Discrepancy worth knowing about.** LeadDev's Dec 2024 coverage quotes Noda saying: *"For every one-point increase in DXI score, you save about **ten minutes** per week per engineer."* (https://leaddev.com/reporting/dx-core-4-aims-to-unify-developer-productivity-frameworks). The published research says 13. If you cite the number, cite 13 and the research page; the 10 appears to be an earlier or rounded figure.

**Evidence base, verbatim:** "based on years of accumulated quantitative and qualitative research, and data from **over 40,000 developers across 800 organizations**. Analyses have included cognitive interviews, descriptive statistics, criterion-related validity analyses, reliability analyses, regression analyses and predictive modeling." Elsewhere: "over four million benchmark samples."

**Other DXI stats:** "top-quartile DXI scores correlate with engineering speed and quality that is **4 to 5 times higher** than bottom-quartile DXI scores"; top-quartile teams score "**43% higher on employee engagement**."

**The 14 dimensions — no public enumeration exists.** DX consistently says "14 dimensions" and gives only partial examples across sources. Named across pages: *deep work, local iteration speed, release process, confidence in making changes, code maintainability, build and test, documentation, code review, CI/CD, clear direction, cross-team collaboration, ease of release, focus time, code quality.* That's ~14 candidates but DX never publishes the canonical list — which is precisely the hook for the black-box criticism in Thread B. The methodology statement is:
> "The 14 dimensions are combined into a single overall DXI score, providing a balanced and transparent indicator that is protected from the volatility of individual metrics."

## A3. ⭐ THE CRITICAL FINDING — DX's stance on individual measurement

**Your hypothesis is half right, and the half that's wrong is the more interesting half.**

DX's *published framework language* contains no carve-out for coaching or outlier identification. It is stated as an absolute prohibition. But DX's *product* ships individual-level metrics, on by default. That gap is the story.

### The framework language is absolute

The load-bearing sentence, from the Speed section of the launch post:
> "The primary metric for Speed is Diffs per Engineer (or PRs per Engineer)… **It is critical that this metric is never used at the individual level or tied to performance evaluations.** Additionally, it must be counterbalanced with other oppositional metrics like the Developer Experience Index (DXI)."
> — Abi Noda, https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/introducing-the-dx-core-4

The three stated preconditions for using diffs per engineer at all: (1) counterbalance with oppositional metrics like DXI; (2) set no targets or rewards tied to them; (3) communicate and roll out so it doesn't get abused.

The framework's own positioning statement:
> "It's critical that leaders position these metrics in a way where they are showing up as **allies to developers**. These metrics are about **helping** developers by understanding their friction points and addressing them."

### Noda saying it's built into the product

From the Kent Beck interview (below), his three-item list of what keeps Core 4 from going bad:
> "1. Communicating and following through on being an ally to developers. 2. **Never measuring metrics like diffs per engineer at the individual level — that's something we stipulate in our framework and build into our product.** 3. Using it within this basket of metrics — developer experience is as important as speed, and quality balances both."
> — Abi Noda, https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/developer-productivity-metrics-the

### On the podcast, both authors say it plainly

DX podcast, "DX Core 4: Framework overview, key design principles" — https://getdx.com/podcast/dx-core-4-framework-overview/
> **Abi Noda:** "This is not measured at the individual level."
> **Laura Tacho:** "We're not intending to measure how many PRs Abi closed last week."
> **Laura Tacho:** "There's some other metrics in the Core 4 framework… I might've said, under no circumstance have that in a metrics framework because the tendency to misuse them was just too high."
> **Abi Noda:** "We definitely viewed this as controversial and had a lot of internal conflict… around its inclusion."
> **Laura Tacho:** "Speed is great, but if you're going faster with being less effective, that's not great… we have these oppositional metrics in place to build in some barriers."

Noda in LeadDev on the same point: *"Engineers don't want to be reduced to lines of code or number of pull requests."* And on the guardrail logic: *"If there are cultural problems created with diffs per engineer, then that will be reflected in the Developer Experience Index."*

### The general guidance page, which is the most explicit anti-individual text DX publishes

https://getdx.com/blog/developer-productivity/ — the "anti-patterns" and "pitfalls" sections, verbatim:
> "**Never tie throughput metrics to individual performance.** Metrics like diffs per engineer should only be used at team or organizational levels to guide improvement discussions."
> "**Avoid vanity metrics and individual targeting.** Never tie throughput metrics like diffs per engineer to individual performance."
> "Story points were designed for team planning, not individual measurement. **Using them for performance evaluation destroys their value as planning tools.** Agile velocity should inform sprint planning, not performance reviews."
> "Measuring how developers spend their time **creates a surveillance culture that undermines trust and creativity**."
> "Pull requests and individual coding activity metrics can be misleading productivity indicators. **They often reward busywork over meaningful contributions.**"

On AI specifically: *"Focus on team-level impact rather than individual AI usage metrics… **never tie AI usage directly to performance evaluations**."* And on agents: *"Should we treat autonomous AI agents as team members? **No** — treat them as extensions of the developers and teams that oversee their work."*

And in the AI measurement hub (https://getdx.com/blog/ai-measurement-hub/):
> "**Always aggregate at team or department level, never track individuals.** This protects psychological safety, avoids perverse incentives, and builds trust."

### ⭐ The tension: DX's product ships a per-individual dashboard, default ON

**This is the finding that most complicates the public stance**, and it's in DX's own docs — https://docs.getdx.com/dashboard/overview/

> "The **Personal dashboard** provides ICs on your team a single spot to easily see relevant information about their PRs, tasks, and **metrics around how they are performing**."

Its "Personal breakdowns" are: **Time allocation** (time across work categories, with trends), **Review activity** (code review count and average turnaround time, with historical trends), and **PR throughput** (pull requests merged). Then:

> "**Configuring individual metrics visibility** — **By default, Dashboard shows individual metrics alongside team metrics.** This can be disabled without affecting other reporting features across DX: Go to DX → Settings → General. Under **Individual metrics visibility**, select whether you want individual metrics enabled for Dashboard or not."

So: individual PR throughput exists in the product, is on by default, and turning it off is an org-admin setting rather than an architectural guarantee. The defensible reading is that it's framed as **self-service for the IC** (the developer seeing their own numbers), not a manager's ranking view — which is exactly the design constraint Swarmia states explicitly and DX does not. That's a real, citable asymmetry between the two vendors, and it's the sharpest question you can put to DX.

**Where the "coaching/outliers" carve-out actually lives:** not in DX's framework, but in **Swarmia's and LinearB's** product positioning (individual views permitted for 1:1 coaching, forbidden for ranking) — see Thread B. If you want a DX-adjacent version of that argument, the closest is Laura Tacho's personal writing, next.

## A4. Laura Tacho — the deepest treatment of individual measurement anywhere in this corpus

**⚠️ Role correction, important for attribution:** Laura Tacho was **CTO at DX from 2023 to 2026** and is now **Senior Principal Technologist, Developer Experience, at AWS** (https://at.linkedin.com/in/lauratacho — "Developer Experience @ AWS, former CTO…"; also her WeAreDevelopers and OSS+ELC EU 2026 speaker bios). She remains Core 4's co-author. Don't describe her as DX's current CTO in anything dated 2026.

### Her canonical piece: "Using Metrics to Measure Individual Developer Performance"
https://lauratacho.com/blog/using-metrics-to-measure-individual-developer-performance

This is the single best-argued practitioner document on the topic, and it is notably **not** an "individual measurement is impossible" polemic. Her opening move is to reject that dodge:

> "A lot of research and 'best practice' will tell us that metrics like lines of code, story points completed, or deployment frequency are not appropriate to measure individual performance. This is true… **Applying them to individuals is unfair at best.** But here's the question we don't talk about enough: '**What data are you going to use to evaluate my performance?**' This is the question that really counts — coming directly from your team members. **There's a better answer than 'best practice says not to use metrics,' which doesn't spark a lot of trust in a fair performance review.**"

Her structural argument:
> "**Software is written by teams, not individuals.** Even if a feature or component is owned by an individual, it's likely that their code depends on systems written by others… **An individual cannot fully control their performance within a system where they are just one contributor.** If the metrics aren't satisfactory, they need to be addressed on a team or system level, not an individual level."

On cross-team comparability:
> "how can you fairly and effectively measure individual performance when teams have different estimation practices? For example, what might be a 3-point story to one team is a 5-point story to another. **So is the individual on the team who calls it a 5-point story a better performer, because they close down more points?**"

The trust argument:
> "**A fast way to reassure your team that you don't understand their job is to pick what they perceive as arbitrary and unfair metrics to measure their performance.**"
> "If I pair with someone and therefore don't commit the code myself, am I penalised? What if I'm working on a design document or coordinating a release? **Responsibilities of developers often go beyond data that can be scraped from GitHub.**"

Goodhart, with her own examples:
> "If you measure a factory based on weight output, expect heavy products. If you measure it based on the number of items produced, expect tiny, tiny products. A practical example: **if the number of commits is a target for individual performance, expect to see some very dirty git histories. You'd probably do the same thing.**"

Her list of metrics that punish the right behavior: "Code coverage is a target, so development hours are spent on writing more tests, but the Change Failure Rate stays the same… **Your team hits aggressive deadlines, but ⅓ of the team resigns within 2 months**… More PRs are closed, but you're not acquiring new customers."

**Her central reframe — the most quotable line in the piece:**
> "**Evidence doesn't have to mean activity data.**"
> "Instead of looking for a list of metrics to determine how you measure performance, **figure out how you want to measure performance and then find metrics that help you measure the stuff that's important to your company.**"

Her worked alternative (derived from an actual job description) uses: project on-time delivery (% delivered ±1 week of forecast), satisfaction with engineering partnership from cross-functional peers, quality/reliability via incident and bug volume, business performance of features via adoption. And crucially:
> "**What I'm not measuring is also important.** I've made a choice here not to directly measure things like PR count, commits, or even story points… **If the value is not there, I might debug why that is with specific activity metrics.**"

**⭐ Her two explicit exceptions — this is the closest thing in the whole corpus to your "individual measurement is OK for specific purposes" hypothesis:**

1. **Seniority-graded metrics.** "It may be perfectly reasonable to look at task-level metrics for a junior engineer, but not for that staff engineer." And: "If I were a Track 4 engineer, I would find it a bit silly/annoying if my commit history was taken into consideration for my performance."
2. **System metrics for people whose job IS the system.** "using team metrics to measure individual performance is generally unfair **unless it's the explicit role of the individual to influence the system performance metrics**. Usually, this happens at a staff+ or management level. If your role's main objective is to support teams by improving performance of CI/CD systems, and you've been given resources, time, and autonomy to do so, **it's reasonable that metrics like Change Failure Rate or Build Time would be used to evaluate how effective you've performed your role**."

Her closing principle: "Focus on outcomes, not output, **but you might use output metrics like activity from GitHub and JIRA to debug why outcomes were missed**."

### ⭐⭐ Tacho personally rolled out GitPrime — and calls it a flop

This is the highest-value bridge between your two threads. From her guest post on The Pragmatic Engineer, "Measuring Software Engineering Productivity" — https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/engineering-productivity

> "When I was a **Senior Director of Engineering at CloudBees** several years ago, **I helped roll out GitPrime to 300+ developers. It was a flop.** (It's worth noting this was prior to GitPrime's acquisition and rebranding to Pluralsight Flow…) Hindsight tells me why: beyond my own mistakes, **the fundamental idea I could boil down productivity to a handful of metrics which look nice on a dashboard, was – and remains – a myth.**"
> "**I learned these lessons the hard – and expensive – way.**… I had pressure from my senior leadership team to quantify performance and report on it. So, **I bought into the idea that quantitative data is always better than qualitative data**, though my teams had plenty to share about what slowed them down."

Also from that piece:
> "**DORA metrics aren't intended to measure the productivity of teams, and certainly never intended to measure the productivity of individuals.** They began as a way to benchmark DevOps adoption across the industry."
> "when you apply this method to systems of humans, you won't get the result you hope for."

**⚠️ Disclosure to carry:** Gergely Orosz states in that same post, "**I am an investor in and an advisor in DX**." That matters when citing Pragmatic Engineer coverage of DX/Core 4 as independent.

### Her verdict on activity metrics, from the DX podcast
https://getdx.com/podcast/measure-developer-productivity/
> "**In zero cases did those Git Metrics, those activity metrics that you can scrape from an API, tell me something that my team wasn't telling me already.**"
> "**People feel very spied on, quite honestly.**"
> "It's surprising, as the logical, rational engineering leader who has a bias toward quantitative, automatically collected data, **how little value that we put on things like perception and sentiment**."
> "My biggest advice is just ask them, because chances are they have the answer."

### Tacho on AI and measurement (2025–2026)

**Talk: "Measuring the Wrong Things Faster Than Ever"**, WeAreDevelopers World Congress — https://www.wearedevelopers.com/world-congress/agenda/sessions/measuring-the-wrong-things-faster-than-ever-1243218. Abstract verbatim:
> "**Tokenmaxxing. Bloated PRs. Endless tiny commits. We already know how easily developer productivity metrics can be gamed. So why are token spend and AI-generated lines of code becoming the default way to measure the impact of agentic coding tools?**"

From the Pragmatic Engineer AI-measurement interview — https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-the-impact-of-ai-on-software:
> "**One of my more controversial opinions is that source code is a liability.**"
> "**Do we really want to measure AI impact in terms of lines of code generated? I certainly don't.**"
> "**Acceptance rate is just such a tiny part of the story.**"
> "**Typing speed has never been the bottleneck in development.** A lot of that time, we're just reallocating to reviewing or other parts of code authoring that's not typing."

From ShiftMag (https://shiftmag.dev/this-cto-says-93-of-developers-use-ai-but-productivity-is-still-10-8013/):
> "**This is really a management problem. The hype made it sound like just trying AI would automatically pay off.**"
> "**I am skeptical of any technology's promise to improve performance without addressing those underlying constraints.**"
> "Transformation is uncomfortable. **Organizations that were ready to quit their cloud or agile transformations are now giving up on AI transformation, too.**"
> Data point: "AI-authored code now makes up **26.9% of all production code** – up from 22% last quarter," across ~4.2M developers, Nov 2025–Feb 2026.

Also widely quoted: *"My biggest advice when trying to navigate this AI paradigm shift that we're in is that **data will beat hype**."*

## A5. Abi Noda's "Flawed Five" — and the direct shot at the individual-scoring vendors

"Five flawed productivity metrics" — https://getdx.com/blog/flawed-productivity-metrics/ (also https://abinoda.com/five-flawed-metrics), from his **GitHub Universe 2019** talk "The elusive quest to measure developer productivity." The five: **commits, lines of code, number of pull requests, velocity points, code impact.**

**⭐ The fifth one is a direct attack on GitPrime/Pluralsight Flow and Code Climate Velocity, quoting their marketing back at them:**
> "**Code impact.** You may not have heard of this metric unless you've explored one of the many engineering metrics vendors out there. Here's a definition of this metric from one such vendor: '*Impact attempts to answer the question, "Roughly how much cognitive load did the engineer carry when implementing these changes?" through the severity of edits to the codebase, as compared to repository history.*' Or from another: '*The magnitude of changes to the codebase over a period of time based on whether code is added or changed, the proximity of the edits to one another, and the specific nature of the change on a line-by-line basis.*' **I'm hesitant to call this metric snake oil because I'm sure it is well-intentioned. But anyone who's ever written a line of code knows that there's no legitimacy to this measure.**"

On commits: "**it is impossible to measure commits with any semblance of accuracy** since developers have unique individual commit patterns and typically squash their commits."

**Companion research review**, "Measuring developer activity: what the research says" (updated Nov 26, 2025) — https://getdx.com/blog/measuring-developer-activity/ — collects the academic case:
- **Collin Green & Ciera Jaspan (Google):** "lines of code per minute will not tell you which software developers are the best."
- **Dr. Margaret-Anne Storey:** warns against focusing on "pull requests, which we do not recommend."
- **Dr. Nicole Forsgren:** "**Rewarding developers for lines of code leads to bloated software**"; metrics "should never be used in isolation."
- **Jaspan & Sadowski (Google):** individual tracking "can create a morale issue" and "bring down overall productivity"; developers fear "misinterpretation by non-technical managers."
- The business-case demolition: managers "**frequently already know who low performers are**" — the tool solves a problem that was never the bottleneck.

Also cited there: **Bryan Finster** (founder of Walmart's DevOps Dojo), on a GitPrime deployment — teams cherry-picked easy tasks, code-review participation *declined*, staff engineers abandoned mentoring, and one team inflated review-comment counts to hit "GitPrime's recommended minimums." His verdict: "**Under no circumstances should this be used.**" And: "'**What gets measured gets managed' isn't a recommendation, it's a warning.**" — https://getdx.com/blog/pitfalls-of-developer-activity-metrics/

## A6. ⭐ The Kent Beck × Abi Noda interview — the best single artifact in Thread A

"Measuring developer productivity: A clear-eyed view," *Engineering Enablement*, **Feb 5, 2025** — https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/developer-productivity-metrics-the (reposted from Kent Beck's blog; the tidyfirst.substack.com URL now redirects to newsletter.kentbeck.com). Subtitle: "**Kent Beck grilled me on Goodhart's Law, benchmarks, and the purpose of measurement.**"

DX **paid Kent Beck to interrogate them** — Noda's framing: *"Kent laughingly said: 'Yep, and the irony of this is that you guys paid me to grill you.'"* And: *"both publicly and privately, Kent has been a staunch and vocal critic of metrics."*

**Beck's opening:**
> "I would like to adopt a new resolution that **any conversation about metrics has to start with Goodhart's Law**… When you pitch metrics, it's in your best interest that people adopt them. How do you navigate both communicating the upside and the potential downside?"

**Beck's sharpest lines:**
> "**It's worse than inaccurate, because people degrade the system to produce the number.**"
> "You have to **genuinely be an ally. This isn't about communication strategy.** There's a kind of sin… It's like, 'Well, how can I make it sound like I'm on the programmer's side? Because if they're convinced I'm on their side, then I'm gonna make a bunch of money, even though I'm screwing them over.'… **If that's your actual goal, you can paint over it with active listening and pretend empathy, but eventually it'll show through and be negative for the world.**"
> "**I would go so far as to say if you just sell the dashboard, that's malpractice.**"
> "You have an educational challenge — an education business with tool support. That's how it has to be, because **if you just sell the tools, it's going to turn bad. Look at the shift in the political climate toward the surveillance economy — that's the societal direction we're going. For creative work, that's a disaster.**"
> On DXI's self-report validity: "**How many developers have actually experienced a really effective development environment? Do they know what really good looks like?**" (his Forest/Desert framing)
> Closing: "**I am afraid of the misuse of this kind of information.**"

**Noda's answers:**
> "Goodhart's Law is 100% true. **As soon as these measures become something folks are incentivized to game and manipulate, the very signal you worked so hard and paid for becomes useless or inaccurate.**"
> The three-guardrail list including "**Never measuring metrics like diffs per engineer at the individual level**" (quoted in full in A3).
> On why it's called "Effectiveness": "**Peggy Ann Storey** [was] like, 'No that should be called developer experience.' **GitHub says it should be called developer happiness.** But it needs to be called effectiveness because that's what we're actually trying to measure — **not developer happiness but effectiveness**… These questions are about workflow friction and process effectiveness, not, '**Do I have enough free beer?**'"
> The anti-productivity reframe, crediting **John Cutler**: "he said **you can't measure productivity but you can measure anti-productivity**. That's the spirit of what we're trying to do with the developer experience index. **We're trying to measure the waste**… versus telling people to go faster."
> Beck's benchmark critique gets the health-metrics analogy: "it's like getting a lipid test but not being able to meet with a physician who can properly interpret it."

## A7. DX's AI measurement work (2025–2026)

**The AI Measurement Framework** — three dimensions: **utilization, impact, cost** (https://getdx.com/blog/how-to-implement-ai-measurement-framework/, https://getdx.com/blog/measure-ai-impact/). Built "in collaboration with researchers, leading AI vendors, and customers"; positioned as research-backed and vendor-agnostic.

- **Utilization:** AI tool usage (DAU/WAU); % of PRs that are AI-assisted; % of committed code that is AI-generated; tasks assigned to agents.
- **Impact:** AI-driven time savings across the SDLC; developer satisfaction with AI tooling; correlations between AI usage and the Core 4; human-equivalent hours completed by autonomous agents.
- **Cost:** least developed — spend imported via custom tables.

**Adoption journey:** "organizations start by focusing on usage, then shift to measuring impact, and finally to understanding and optimizing ROI."

**⚠️ An internal inconsistency worth noting:** the AI hub says "Always aggregate at team or department level, never track individuals," while the implementation guide's 6-month rollout plan says "**Track weekly adoption at the team and individual levels**" and "Segment users into cohorts (heavy, frequent, occasional, non-users)… **document what high-performing users are doing**." Defensible as enablement research rather than evaluation, but it is individual-level tracking, and it's in the same product's docs.

**Reports:** "State of AI Impact in Engineering" quarterly, 500+ engineering orgs, combining telemetry with survey across Core 4 + the AI framework (https://getdx.com/news/dx-releases-q2-2026-state-of-ai-impact-in-engineering-report/). Headline: median quarterly AI spend grew ~**$1.5K → $44K in a year, ~28x**, in Tech alone — "spend is scaling far faster than the outcomes it's meant to justify."

### ⭐ "Revisiting the DX Core 4 in the age of AI" — Brian Houck, June 24, 2026
https://newsletter.getdx.com/p/revisiting-the-dx-core-4 — note the byline: **Brian Houck**, a SPACE co-author, now writing DX's newsletter. This is the most current official position, and it re-states the individual prohibition **more concessively than the 2024 launch did**:

> "**The criticism of PR throughput is entirely fair at the individual level.** Not all PRs are created equal in terms of size, complexity, or value. DX developed a methodology called **TrueThroughput**, which uses AI to normalize these variations by weighting PRs based on actual complexity. **Yet, even with that kind of normalization in place, the metric is a poor instrument for evaluating any individual developer's contribution. I've argued this myself, and I'd stand by it. Using PR throughput to assess individuals is the wrong application of the metric.**"

That's notable: DX built an AI complexity-normalization layer (TrueThroughput) — the obvious technical route to "now we *can* score individuals fairly" — and then explicitly declines to make that claim.

Other key lines:
> "**AI doesn't change what engineering organizations are trying to accomplish. What it does is make the signals noisier.**"
> "**Pull request counts spike, cycle times compress, and code volumes bloat.** Engineering leaders who chase these surface-level fluctuations… **risk optimizing for sheer motion rather than actual progress.**"
> "**Tracking AI telemetry tells us how the work is changing. Tracking the core dimensions tells us if that change is actually delivering results.**"
> "**When leaders are tasked with proving AI investment ROI, they cannot do it by pointing to adoption spikes or token volume. A high utilization rate means nothing if software delivery stalls or system stability crashes.**"
> The two best AI-era interpretation puzzles: "**PR Merge Rate:** … In an agentic workflow, does a 95% merge rate mean the AI is flawless? **Or does it mean your human developers are rubber-stamping machine-generated code because they're too overwhelmed to properly review it?**" And "**Time-to-10th-PR:** … if an AI onboarding assistant can help an engineer generate and ship 10 PRs by their second afternoon, does that metric still capture true structural onboarding health? **Or does it just track how quickly someone learned to use AI tools?**"
> DX's own longitudinal finding: AI coding tools produced "roughly a **7.8% increase in PR throughput**" — "**a useful corrective to more optimistic claims about AI's productivity impact.**" And "during the first quarter of 2026, the percentage of code generated by AI that reaches production is **27.4%** of production code on average."
> Closing: "**The framework is stable. The interpretation is where the real work begins.**"

He also flags a possible successor metric: **"Idea-to-Customer" velocity from the EngThrive framework paper**, "one implementation worth watching as a future key metric for the speed dimension."

# THREAD B — the competitive and critical landscape

## B1. GitPrime → Pluralsight Flow: the canonical cautionary tale

### Timeline
| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 2015 | GitPrime founded (YC W16), CEO Travis Kimmel |
| **May 1, 2019** | Pluralsight acquires GitPrime for **$170M all cash** — https://techcrunch.com/2019/05/01/pluralsight-will-acquire-gitprime-for-170m/ · HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19802067 |
| May 2019 | Earnings call: "$170 million… approximately **5 times to 6 times expected 2020 billings**"; GitPrime had "only… a **few hundred customers**" |
| ~2020 | Rebranded **Pluralsight Flow** |
| Dec 2020 | Vista Equity takes Pluralsight private, **$3.5B** |
| **May 31, 2024** | Vista **writes Pluralsight's equity to zero**, hands it to creditors — https://www.axios.com/2024/05/31/vista-equity-pluralsight · HN: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40536960 |
| **Feb 2025** | **Appfire acquires Flow** |
| **Jun 30, 2026** | Renewals closed |
| **Dec 31, 2027** | **End of life** — "Appfire will retire Flow… no longer be available for purchase or use" |

$170M → three owners in six years → equity to zero → retirement announced. **Precision note:** Flow is not dead *yet* — it runs to Dec 2027. Say "sunset announced," not "shut down." Migration wrinkle: historical data doesn't migrate, and Flow's proprietary "Coding Days" and "Impact" have no equivalent elsewhere.

### What it measured
Per GitClear's four-way comparison (Feb 2021, https://www.gitclear.com/pluralsight_gitclear_pinpoint_code_climate_code_development_kpi_metric_alternatives): lines of code → "Impact/Diff Delta," "Code Churn," "Efficiency"; issues/PRs → cycle time, throughput, lead time; commits → "Active Days." GitClear's own verdict on commits: "**a dicey data source**" with "**no intrinsic signal**," and "**the most trivially 'gameable' of the three data sources.**"

Churn's actual definition, from a user: "**modifying a line that had been previously modified in the last month**" (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=19929459). And the individual view — **"Developer360" profiles** — was never removed; it was a selling feature to the end (cited as a Flow differentiator on Jellyfish's own competitive page, https://jellyfish.co/blog/waydev-alternatives/).

For example, **replacing old code with new code was penalized as 'code churn', so we had to write something like `if (false) { // old code } // new code`**. ## B2. The rest of the vendor landscape — who scores individuals

### Code Climate Velocity — ⚠️ the popular claim is half wrong
What shut down was the **free tier, "Velocity for Teams"**: announced Dec 2023, accounts deactivated and **data deleted March 18, 2024**. Paid/enterprise subscriptions were unaffected. Separately, Code Climate Quality was spun out as a new company, **Qlty Software**. Don't say "Code Climate Velocity shut down" without that qualifier. CEO Bryan Helmkamp's public defense of the category is a good primary source for vendor framing (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23095725): "engineers inherently want to be productive… it can be quite difficult to get visibility into roadblocks… **especially for managers who are one or two levels removed from programming**."

### ⭐ Swarmia — the loudest anti-individual stance, and the one enforced in product architecture
https://www.swarmia.com/git-analytics/:
> "**Just because something is easy to measure doesn't mean it should be tracked.** We've **intentionally left out** traditional Git analytics metrics like the following: **Lines of code (LOC), Code churn and rework, Developer stack ranking.**"
> "**In Swarmia, you won't see leaderboards ranking developers or teams from best to worst.**"
> "**The best teams focus on team performance, not individual performance. Swarmia is not a tool for stalking developers.**"

**⭐ This is the precise articulation of your "individual view for coaching, not ranking" hypothesis** — Hugo Kiiski, Mar 15, 2023, https://www.swarmia.com/blog/bringing-visibility-into-a-developers-work/. Three explicit product constraints: Swarmia will **not** allow comparing individuals side by side; will **not** expose an individual's code metrics (LOC, PR throughput); and will **not** limit access to managers only (the developer sees their own view). Rationale: "**These metrics are too situational to draw conclusions from, and do more harm than good when evaluating an individual.**"

**Otto Hilska (founder/CEO), "So, you'd like to stack rank your developers?", Sep 26, 2025** — https://www.swarmia.com/blog/dont-stack-rank-your-developers/:
> "**Stack ranking doesn't deliver what it promises. Instead of objectivity, you get gaming.**"
> "**Knowledge becomes currency. Developers stop documenting their work, and they avoid doing things like pair programming.**"
> "**The developers you most want to keep are the first to leave.**"
> "**Some vendors in this space will still try to sell you a single number or normalized 'productivity score' — which is often just lines of code with a few extra steps**, dressed up in a bow tie."
> "the developer who writes 100 lines of elegant, maintainable code creates more value than the one who writes 500 lines" destined for refactoring.
> "**To truly coach someone to do better, you will have to talk about the work — not the numbers.**"
> Cycle time, a good team metric, is "**useless for evaluating individuals**."

**Rebecca Murphey** (then Field CTO), Jul 23, 2025, https://www.swarmia.com/blog/developer-productivity-metrics-missing-the-point/: activity metrics "**don't only fail to capture what matters, but actively make things worse**"; developers hear "developer productivity" and "**imagine being reduced to a number**." Also: "**Metrics are the lagging indicator… They are great discussion-starters, and bad conclusions.**"

Extended to AI: "**Swarmia AI doesn't measure individual productivity, performance, or competence.**" (https://help.swarmia.com/features/swarmia-ai)

### ⭐ Waydev — the sharpest gap between marketing copy and product architecture
Historically the archetype of individual roll-up scoring (named alongside GitPrime by GitSense's founder and in a 2020 Ask HN listing exactly two tools). The product **still ships** a "**For Contributors**" section — "**Keep track of your own performance**" — and "**Contributor Insights**" (https://waydev.co/measure-developer-productivity/).

But its current content marketing argues against individual reporting in nearly Swarmia's language:
> "**Board dashboards should track teams, products, and value streams rather than individual developers. Individual activity counts can distort behavior and miss work such as planning, review, incident response, or mentoring.**" — https://waydev.co/key-metrics-to-include-on-a-board-level-engineering-dashboard/
> "**Don't use metrics to micromanage. They're tools for support, not surveillance.**"

**The gap between "we ship Contributor Insights" and "don't rank individuals" is the story.** Waydev's guardrail is documentation; Swarmia's is product architecture. DX sits in between — a policy statement plus a default-on toggle.

https://linearb.io/blog/developer-productivity-metrics:
> "Some companies and leaders focus on **output metrics like lines of code to stack rank devs**, rather than gaining visibility into the process–*cough cough* **Elon Musk**. This approach is great…**for killing productivity, diminishing motivation, and creating a bad habit of gaming outputs**."

### Jellyfish
Positions as team/business alignment. Secondary summaries say it provides "visibility into individual trends for better 1:1 coaching." **⚠️ Not first-party verified** — their relevant blog and library URLs 404'd. Don't quote a Jellyfish stance without a live source.

### ⭐ Faros AI — the best 2026-dated framing of the whole problem
**Thierry Donneau-Golencer, Jan 5, 2026** — https://www.faros.ai/blog/lines-of-code-metric-ai-vanity-outcome:
> "**Lines of code was already a discredited productivity metric.**"
> "**The best developers often ship features by removing code, not adding it.**"
> Their finding: developers on high-AI-adoption teams completed "**21% more tasks and merging 98% more pull requests**," but orgs saw "**no measurable improvement in delivery outcomes**."

That last pair is the sharpest 2026 formulation available: **individual metrics can rise while the system delivers nothing more.** It's the empirical bridge from Thread B back to Core 4's counterbalancing logic.

### Uplevel — and the Copilot study
Uplevel's public writing is team/system framed with no explicit individual-vs-team position. **The Copilot study** (Sept 2024, https://resources.uplevelteam.com/gen-ai-for-coding): ~800 developers (351 in the Copilot group), ~3-month baseline vs. follow-up. **Headline: "The group using Copilot introduced 41% more bugs, suggesting Copilot might affect code quality, given it didn't affect PR throughput."** Burnout: non-Copilot devs cut extended hours 28%, Copilot users only 17%.
**⚠️ Carry the caveat:** it measured Copilot *access*, not usage; critic Jason St-Cyr questions whether it's "a genuine issue or merely marketing for Uplevel's competing products" (https://jasonstcyr.com/2024/10/09/does-github-copilot-actually-raise-bugs-in-code-by-41/); GitHub's own Nov 2024 research claims quality gains. The irony worth naming: **an engineering-intelligence vendor used aggregate metrics to debunk a productivity claim** — the defensible use of the very data that turns toxic at the individual level.

### ⭐ Dev Interrupted (LinearB) vs. Core 4 — the direct competitive attack
**Ben Lloyd Pearson, "Core 4 fails the vanity metric test," Jul 24, 2025** — https://devinterrupted.substack.com/p/core-4-fails-the-vanity-metric-test. This is the most substantive vendor-side attack on Core 4 and you should expect it in any competitive conversation.

> "**I wonder how much better off we might be if we focused less on creating academic frameworks like Core 4.**… Why do we need another framework that repackages existing metrics while adding problematic new ones? **The answer is that there's money to be made in creating proprietary measurement systems that require expensive consulting engagements and specialized tooling to implement.**"

He applies **John Cutler's** eight vanity-metric criteria (actionable, timely, contextual, aligned, unambiguous, gaming-resistant, drives right behavior, comparable), defining vanity metrics as those that "**make us feel good but don't help us do better work or make better decisions.**"

**On the DXI — "the ultimate black box":**
> "Perhaps the most egregious example in Core 4 is the Developer Experience Index: **a proprietary composite metric based on survey responses that fails virtually every criterion for meaningful measurement.**"
> "**Black box proprietary formula makes it impossible to know what actions will improve it.**"
> "When executives ask how improving your DXI score will drive bottom-line growth, what's your answer? '**Well, we don't know how it's calculated, but the consultants say it's important.**'"
> "**If your productivity measurement requires a specific tool to calculate, you're not measuring productivity; you're measuring vendor lock-in.**"

**On PRs per engineer:**
> "**It's the epitome of effort-based measurement that misses the point entirely.**"
> "**This approach encourages stack-ranking developers based on activity rather than value creation, which is a culture killer that drives away your best talent.**"
> "**measuring effort without measuring outcomes is like judging a chef by how many ingredients they use rather than how the food tastes.**"
> His concession — the two conditions under which elite teams legitimately use effort metrics: "(1) They are conducting controlled experiments, in which they have isolated all other factors… (2) They have an extremely high degree of trust that the metric won't be gamed because it is not factored into the overall productivity analysis. **However, the typical engineering team doesn't always have the resources for the first scenario, and it's extremely difficult to build the culture and psychological safety needed for the second.**"

**On revenue per engineer** (a Core 4 secondary metric): "**fails every single criterion**"; "**Incentivizes headcount reduction over value creation**"; "**Easily gamed by reducing headcount or reclassifying roles**"; "**Promotes fear and internal competition rather than collaboration.**"

**On perception metrics:** "**Your most vocal critics might be your highest performers, while your quietest team could be struggling but afraid to speak up.**"

**His summary charge:** "**Core 4 took these proven metrics and layered problematic new ones on top, creating a framework that's worse than the sum of its parts.**" And: "**The rest is just consultant theater.**"

**Note the symmetry to flag:** Dev Interrupted is LinearB's publication, and LinearB is a direct Core 4 competitor that *also* publishes a "DX Core 4 deep dive" implementation guide (https://linearb.io/blog/dx-core-4-deep-dive). Read the critique as competitive positioning — but the DXI black-box argument stands on its own merits, since DX genuinely does not publish the 14-item list or the scoring formula.

## B3. McKinsey (2023) and the backlash

### The article
**"Yes, you can measure software developer productivity," Aug 17, 2023** — https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/technology-media-and-telecommunications/our-insights/yes-you-can-measure-software-developer-productivity

**⚠️ Byline correction:** the authors are **Chandra Gnanasambandam, Martin Harrysson, Alharith Hussin, Jason Keovichit, and Shivam Srivastava**. **Wenjie Wu is not an author** of this piece. Dan North notes "all five contributing authors are male."

**Framing claims, verbatim:**
> "**Compared with other critical business functions such as sales or customer operations, software development is perennially undermeasured.**"
> "**The long-held belief by many in tech is that it's not possible to do it correctly**—and that, in any case, only trained engineers are knowledgeable enough to assess the performance of their peers. **Yet that status quo is no longer sustainable.**"
> Gen-AI: tools "have the potential to enable developers to complete tasks **up to two times faster**."
> Evidence base: "implemented at **nearly 20** tech, finance, and pharmaceutical companies, and the initial results are promising."

**Their explicit individual-level language:**
> "it's essential to understand the three types of metrics that need to be tracked: those at the **system level, the team level, and the individual level**."
> "while deployment frequency is a perfectly good metric to assess systems or teams… it is **not a useful way to track individual performance**."

**The four proprietary additions, layered on DORA/SPACE:**
1. **Inner/outer loop time.** "**maximizing the amount of time developers spend in the inner loop is desirable**… Outer-loop activities are seen by most developers as necessary but **generally unsatisfying chores**." Target: "**Top tech companies aim for developers to spend up to 70 percent of their time doing inner-loop activities.**" Named "low-value-added tasks": provisioning infrastructure, running manual unit tests, managing test data.
2. **Developer Velocity Index (DVI)** benchmark survey.
3. **⭐ Contribution analysis** — the lightning rod: "**Assessing contributions by individuals to a team's backlog** (starting with data from backlog management tools such as Jira, and **normalizing data using a proprietary algorithm**)…" The example: "one company found that **its most talented developers were spending excessive time on noncoding activities such as design sessions or managing interdependencies across teams.** In response, the company changed its operating model… **to enable those highest-value developers to do what they do best: code.**"
4. **Talent capability score** — "**organizations should aspire to a 'diamond' distribution of proficiency**, with the majority of developers in the middle range of competency."

The sentence that drew the most fire: "**leaders and developers alike need to move past the outdated notion that leaders 'cannot' understand the intricacies of software engineering, or that engineering is too complex to measure.**"

**⚠️ McKinsey cites DORA and SPACE but never cites Nicole Forsgren or any coauthor** — the charge North presses hardest.

| P2 (Kent Beck) | Aug 31, 2023 | https://newsletter.kentbeck.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-440 |
| Sequel (Orosz + Abi Noda, 17 companies) | Jan 16, 2024 | https://newsletter.pragmaticengineer.com/p/measuring-developer-productivity-bae |

Parts 1 and most of Part 2 are written "with one, shared voice."

**Beck's precursor posts (LinkedIn, Aug 2023):**
> "**McKinsey claims it's possible to measure developer productivity. The report is so absurd & naive that it makes no sense to critique it in detail.**" — https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinsey-claims-its-possible-to-measure-activity-7099764438496407552-v8P2
> "**McKinsey folks are smart. They know that their intended market wants this report to be good advice, wants to act this way, wants McKinsey's help/permission to do so.**"
> "**What they published damages people I care about. I'm here to help geeks feel safe in the world. This kind of surveillance makes geeks feel less safe.**"
> ⭐ The surgeon analogy: "**McKinsey's 'you can measure developer productivity' is like if we measured surgeon productivity on what percentage of their time they were cutting with a scalpel or stitching with a needle and we ignored whether the patient got better.**" — https://www.linkedin.com/posts/kentbeck_mckinseys-you-can-measure-developer-productivity-activity-7101918867161051136-b8F4

**⭐⭐ Beck's Facebook survey death-spiral — the best single narrative on how measurement corrupts (verbatim, his first person):**
> "At Facebook we instituted the sorts of surveys McKinsey recommends. That was good for about a year… Then folks decided that they wanted to make the survey results more legible… They computed an overall score. Very reasonable thing to do. That was good for another year… **Then those scores started cropping up in performance reviews**… Then those scores started getting rolled up. A manager's score was the average of their reports' scores. A director's score would be the average of their reporting managers' scores. **Now things started getting unhinged.** Directors put pressure on managers for better scores. Managers started negotiating with individual contributors for better survey scores. '**Give me a 5 & I'll make sure you get an "exceeds expectations".**' Directors started cutting managers & teams with poor scores, whether those cuts made organizational sense or not."
> Their summary: "**Things went from, 'we'd like to know how things are going,' to, 'we know even less about how things are going. But they are definitely going worse because people are now gaming the system.'**"

**The political read of why the article exists:**
> "**CEOs and CFOs are increasingly frustrated by CTOs throwing up their hands and saying software engineering is too nuanced to measure, when sales teams have individual measurements and quotas to hit… The executive reasoning goes: if other groups can measure individual performance, it's absurd that engineering cannot.**"
> "If they try to [avoid the question], they risk the CEO or CFO turning instead to McKinsey, who will bring their custom framework, deploy it – even as the CTO protests…"
> "**The McKinsey framework will most likely do far more harm than good to organizations – and to the engineering culture at companies. Such damage could take years to undo.**"
> "keep in mind they're written for a very different, and specific, audience: **untechnical CEOs and CFOs with little to zero experience with software development. Engineering is just another department.**"

**⭐ The core analytical move — effort → output → outcome → impact:**
> "**One critique of McKinsey's system we have is that nearly every one of its custom metrics which differ from DORA and SPACE metrics, measure effort or output.**" (Their exhibit: 4 of 5.)
> "**First, the only folks who care about these metrics are the people collecting them. Customers don't care. Executives don't care. Investors don't care. Second, and most crucially, collecting & evaluating these metrics hinders the measures downstream folks actually do care about, like profitability.**"
> "**The earlier in the cycle you measure, the easier it is to measure. And also the more likely that you introduce unintended consequences.**"
> Their positive proposal: "**Producing at least one customer-facing thing per team, per week.** This output might not sound so impressive, but in practice is very hard to achieve."

**Beck's sales-vs-engineering anecdote:** sales leader — *"'My team's target for the quarter was $600K, and we delivered $520K. I take accountability for the miss…'"* vs. engineering — *"'So, this quarter we shipped Feature A, and we are slightly behind on some tech debt migration…'"* — "**My goodness, the contrast was stark.**"

**Orosz's Uber footnote:** after shipping an Eng Metrics dashboard, "**the lines of code did not change drastically, but the CI systems saw a visible increase in utilization.** Basically, people started to create far, far more diffs, which put a much larger load on the continuous integration (CI) systems, and increased CI costs."

**Part 2 — the sports argument:**
> "**Individual performance does not directly predict team performance. And if it's not possible to deduct team performance from individual performance in a domain that's as easy to measure as sports, then we can expect even less success in software engineering.**"
> "**Team performance is easier to measure than individual performance.**"

**⭐ Orosz's own closing answer:**
> "**Know that measurement interferes with the system.** Every new thing you start measuring will lead to engineers optimizing to make that measure look better. **The more you measure, the more you shape the culture and how people work.**"
> "**Be skeptical when consultants claim it is possible to measure without impacting how people work. It never is.**"
> His gaming taxonomy: "Measure effort: **create high-effort busywork of dubious value** / Measure output: **increase the quantity of the output by what's easiest to do** / Measure outcomes: **aim to beat targets, even if this means taking shortcuts** / Measure impact: **get creative in reaching this with less effort and output.**"
> "**Yes, you can measure developer productivity, but at what cost?** McKinsey is not wrong to state developer productivity can be measured. **However, they avoid the question of what is the cost of the measurements.**"
> "**Attributing this impact to individual engineers is also possible, but the more granular you make the attribution, the more this interferes with incentives, and the more likely you are to create an organization which incentivizes busywork.**"
> "**My suggestion is that if you measure, then start with impact. Not individual impact: but team impact.**"
> "**Take two teams. Team A: communicates their impact clearly, and has a hands-on leader. Team B: has fancy metrics and a hands-off leader. I will take Team A over Team B, anytime.**"

**⭐⭐ Beck's own closing bullets — the most quotable material in the entire series** (his subtitle is sharper than Gergely's: "**They only measure activity, not productivity from a business perspective. And measuring activity comes with costs & risks they do not address.**"):
> "**Be clear about why you are asking & what your power relationship is with the person or people being measured. When the person with power is measuring the person without, you're going to get distortions.**"
> "**Avoid perverse incentives by analyzing data at the same level as you collect the data. I can analyze my own data. My team can analyze its own aggregated data.**"
> "**If you choose to create incentives (broadly defined—money, status, promotion, autonomy) around measures, know that you will never again receive accurate data.**"
> "**Red Team any incentives.** What would a clever (you hired them, of course they are clever), motivated person do to make the numbers look better. **How much damage could they cause in the process.**"
> "**Get comfortable with your own judgement. Executives relying unnecessarily on 'data' seem to be running from responsibility. Grasp that nettle.**"
> "**Measure developer productivity? Not possible.** There are too many confounding factors, network effects, variance, observation effects, and feedback loops to get sensible answers to questions like, '**How many times more profit did Joan create than Harry?**'… **You can measure activity, but not without directing that activity away from the ends you care about.**"
> "**Be suspicious of anyone claiming to measure developer productivity. Ask who is asking & why. Ask them what unit they are measuring & how those units are connected to profit.**"
> "**I am 100% pro-accountability. Weekly delivery of customer-appreciated value is the best accountability, the most aligned, the least distorting.**"

That second bullet — "**analyzing data at the same level as you collect the data**" — is the cleanest available principle for adjudicating the individual-measurement question, and it is exactly what Swarmia implemented in product and what DX's default-on Personal dashboard *arguably* satisfies (the IC sees their own data) but its org-admin toggle does not guarantee.

### ⭐ Dan North — the most detailed technical review
**"McKinsey Developer Productivity Review," Oct 4, 2023** — https://dannorth.net/blog/mckinsey-review/

**⚠️ Correction: there is no Dan North post titled "Do you really want to know…?"** on this topic. The two relevant pieces are this review and "The Worst Programmer I Know."

Written as an open peer review — "*Dear Chandra and team,*" — noting "**I have not seen anyone engage with the content of the article itself.**"

**His two "erroneous planks":**
> "**1. Software development is a reducible activity, and can be measured with reductionist tools. 2. Software development is primarily about coding, and anything other than typing code into a computer terminal is waste which we should seek to eliminate.**"

**On "undermeasured":**
> "**Software development is one of the most ruthlessly scrutinized and measured of all business activities.**"
> "**The one thing you cannot call this era is under-measured. Mis-measured, for sure… but never under-measured!**"
> "**This assumption that software development has the same reducible complexity as assembling a car lies at the heart of the developer productivity challenge.**"

**On the 2x Gen-AI claim:**
> "**most of programming is not typing code.** Most of programming is learning the business domain; understanding the problem; assessing possible solutions; validating assumptions through feedback and experimentation; identifying, assessing and meeting cross-functional needs such as compliance, security, availability, resilience, accessibility, usability… **the typing-the-code part is only a modest part of all of this, so using Gen-AI to speed that up, while useful, is hardly 'making developers twice as fast'.**"

**On the evidence base:** invokes Kahneman's Law of Small Numbers, notes "**no control basis**," that they "**fail to consider the Hawthorne Effect**," asks "**Is this approach causal, just correlated, or coincidental?**"

**On the missing citation:**
> "you fail to cite Dr. Nicole Forsgren, the lead researcher on both initiatives, or any of her coauthors… **our industry has a history of erasing female contributors to software engineering**, so I presume you will rectify this in the next revision."

**⭐ On Contribution Analysis — the demolition:**
> "**This whole segment, which appears to be a cornerstone of the paper, is unfortunately simply misguided. It falls into the fallacy that software development is reducible, like building a wall, where you can measure who lays the most bricks.**"
> "**those who contribute less code to solve the same problem, or even who remove unnecessary or redundant code, are often your highest-value developers.**"
> On "enable those highest-value developers to code": "**And this is the nub of the whole article. Your highest-value developers are 10x by enabling other developers! Often the least useful thing they can be doing is producing code themselves.**"
> "**You appear to be adopting a simplistic model where senior people just do what junior people do but more so, which means the goal is to keep their hands to the keyboard. The whole push of the article is that the best developers should be doing rather than thinking or supporting.**"
> "the backlog… **makes no sense to use it for individual policing.**"

**On inner/outer loop:**
> "**They certainly do not reflect my experience of enterprise software development.**"
> "**The idea that security or compliance audits and requirements are a separate review activity in some outer loop is in direct conflict with the principle of shifting left that McKinsey promotes.**"
> "**Meetings, too, are not an outer loop activity. Any collaboration is a meeting! Pair-programming is a continual meeting…**"
> On test data as "low-value": he recounts an ISP that "**accidentally emailed 16,000 active subscribers to tell them that their broadband was being terminated by using real addresses in a test run.**"

**On Talent Capability Score:**
> "**This is the same error that we find in stack-ranking of teams. In a high-performing team, all the players are on one end of the curve! There is no normal distribution and there is no 'weakest link'.**"

**⭐⭐ His most-quoted line:**
> "**However, attempting to measure the individual contribution of a person is like trying to measure the individual contribution of a piston in an engine. The question itself makes no sense.**"
> And: "**Applying reductionist thinking and tooling is a category error. 'Better' reductionist tooling is just doubling down on doing the wrong thing with the illusion of rigour.**"

**On the self-contradiction:** "**Then you conclude that measuring productivity is contextual, while the entire article is promoting your context-free assessment tooling.**"

**His alternative framing:**
> "**if someone is identified as a 'weak' performer, I take that as signal that we are letting that person down.**"
> "**If the mindset is 'weeding out poor performers' then this suggests an abdication of responsibility; the idea that the flower is at fault for failing to grow rather than the soil or climate.**"

**⚠️ North appended a correction:** "I misread the section *Avoiding metrics missteps*, which in fact says to 'move past the outdated notion that […] engineering is too complex to measure.' However, my point stands…" — cite him honestly on this.

### ⭐ Dan North, "The Worst Programmer I Know," Sept 2, 2023
https://dannorth.net/blog/the-worst-programmer/ — the companion parable about **Tim Mackinnon**, scored on story points at a Big Bank:
> "**Tim's score was consistently zero. Zero! Not just low, or trending downwards, but literally zero.**" (He never signed up for stories: "Instead he would spend his day pairing with different teammates.")
> "**Tim wasn't delivering software; Tim was delivering a team that was delivering software.**"
> "**The entire team became more effective, more productive, more aligned, more idiomatic, more fun, because Tim was in the team.**"
> "**Don't try to measure the individual contribution of a unit in a complex adaptive system, because the premise of the question is flawed.**"

### Other credible critics
- **Grady Booch**, Aug 20, 2023, quote-tweeting the article: "**Ah. This from McKinsey. It's rubbish.**"
- **Dave Farley** (in LeadDev): "**Apart from the use of DORA metrics in this model, the rest is pretty much astrology**" and "**Measuring software development in terms of individual developer productivity is a terrible idea.**"
- **Charity Majors**, July 2020 (predates but is the canonical text the backlash leaned on) — https://charity.wtf/2020/07/07/questionable-advice-can-engineering-productivity-be-measured/: "**The right way to look at performance is at the team level. Individual engineers don't own or maintain code; teams do. The team is the irreducible unit of ownership.**" · "**Some of the hardest and most impactful engineering work will be all but invisible on any set of individual metrics.**" · "**The more challenging and novel a problem, the less reliable these metrics will be. In fact, to the extent you can reduce a job to a set of metrics, that job can be automated away.**"
- **Kelly Vaughn** (Dir. Eng, Spot AI) and **Ori Keren** (CEO, LinearB), Dev Interrupted #147 — https://linearb.io/dev-interrupted/podcast/the-mckinsey-developer-productivity-debate:
  > **Keren:** "the best engineers that I've worked with, **they're the best readers of code**… **if you just let them code, you miss some of their greatest qualities.**" (a direct hit on Contribution Analysis)
  > **Vaughn:** "**I feel strongly that you cannot use a system to measure individual metrics. It's almost like creating an autoimmune system that attacks its own culture.**"
- **Jennifer Riggins, LeadDev, Oct 23, 2023** — best journalistic roundup: https://leaddev.com/career-development/what-mckinsey-got-wrong-about-developer-productivity
- **ShiftMag, Aug 24, 2023** — earliest aggregation, source of the Booch quote: https://shiftmag.dev/mckinsey-measure-developer-productivity-1166/
- **HN thread** (hit #1): https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37203108 · thread on North's review where he participated: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=37800249
- **Abi Noda** was quoted in Orosz's Part 2 with the constructive counter-frame: "*What the CEO wants is to know you're being a good steward of their investment in engineering. You can demonstrate strong stewardship by providing a full picture of engineering, including: Business impact / System performance / And developer effectiveness.*" He then supplied the empirical counter-evidence in the Jan 2024 Pragmatic Engineer piece on what 17 companies actually measure — **which is the direct precursor to Core 4 eleven months later.**

**⚠️ Negative findings — do not attribute:**
- **Marc Andreessen: nothing.** No public response. The 2023 hits are all his "Techno-Optimist Manifesto," unrelated.
- **Titus Winters: nothing found.**
- **Nicole Forsgren: no direct public rebuttal found.** Her role is as the *uncited* author, not a responder. Don't quote her as a McKinsey critic without a source.

## B4. Documented ranking/firing cases

**⚠️ There is no published, named-company, on-the-record case of a layoff executed via GitPrime/Flow/Waydev output.** What exists is (a) consistent first-person testimony that these tools fed reviews and stack ranks (quoted in B1), and (b) named metric-driven ranking cases using other instruments. Frame it that way.

**The mechanism, non-tool-specific but identical** (InsideOutSanta, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42039648):
> "I worked at a major financial supplier whose CEO was super into metrics, and **fired hundreds of the 'worst performers' every year based on his spreadsheet. Like clockwork, every year, I saw the most valuable people in every team get fired**, because those were people who had a deep knowledge of the system, and were often diverted from doing 'visible' work by helping less knowledgeable people. They were the ones who trained new hires, who you went to when you couldn't figure out how to debug your problem, who wrote the architecture documentation… **Guess what, none of this stuff showed up in any spreadsheets.**"

The "Suits" parable version (zem, https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42039765): an associate ranked near the bottom turned out to sit adjacent to the top five, because he was the one helping them — "**there were no metrics for 'helped someone else out but didn't get credit for it'.**"

**⚠️ Twitter/X, Nov 2022 (Musk, LOC-based evaluation): verify independently before publishing.** The only citable-and-verified reference obtained is LinearB's own blog naming him. Primary news sources (Verge, Ars, Business Insider) were unfetchable in this session.

**Context (secondary, mechanism not attributed to any analytics tool):** Meta ~3,600 roles cut Feb 2025 framed as a 5% performance-based reduction; Microsoft ~6,000 in May 2025 with software-engineering focus, ~9,000 in July 2025; layoffs.fyi counts 152,000+ across 551 companies in 2024. Relatedly, and directly on-topic: **Meta stated that individual AI usage/adoption metrics would not be included in 2025 annual performance reviews.**

## B5. The general critique base

**Goodhart / Campbell** is the universal frame — Beck demands every metrics conversation open with it; Tacho builds her factory-weight example on it; the HN commenters arrive at it independently. **Bryan Finster's inversion is the sharpest phrasing:** "'**What gets measured gets managed' isn't a recommendation, it's a warning.**" The **Cobra effect** also appears: "**don't be surprised if developers create or use tools to optimize their changes for the metrics rather than add value to the codebase.**" (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=23208817)

**The Bill Gates line** — "**Measuring programming progress by lines of code is like measuring aircraft building progress by weight**" — ⚠️ treat as apocryphal-but-canonical; even Faros hedges it as "reportedly." Its empirical companion is **Bill Atkinson's "-2000 lines of code"** (https://www.folklore.org/Negative_2000_Lines_Of_Code.html), invoked on HN as: "**I want the '-2000 lines of code' guy, not the one who's best at gaming whatever metrics you use.**" (https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=42039141)

**SPACE** (Forsgren, Storey, Maddila, Zimmermann, Butler, Houck; ACM Queue 2021) — its own guidance is to understand and improve the *system*, not score individuals, and it warns against any single metric or dimension in isolation. https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/the-space-of-developer-productivity-theres-more-to-it-than-you-think/

---

# Synthesis: the four positions on individual measurement

Everyone in this debate agrees activity metrics fail at the individual level. They disagree on what follows.

1. **Absolute prohibition (DX's published framework, Beck, North, Majors).** North: individual contribution is "like trying to measure the individual contribution of a piston in an engine." Beck: "Measure developer productivity? Not possible." DX: "never used at the individual level or tied to performance evaluations." The vulnerability: it leaves Tacho's question — "*What data are you going to use to evaluate my performance?*" — unanswered, and she calls that a trust failure.

2. **Level-matching (Beck's operational rule, Swarmia's architecture).** Beck: "**analyze data at the same level as you collect the data. I can analyze my own data. My team can analyze its own aggregated data.**" Swarmia implements exactly this: the developer sees their own view; no side-by-side comparison; no manager-only access. This is the most defensible position and the one your Core 4 hypothesis was reaching for — but note it lives at **Swarmia**, not DX.

3. **Scoped exceptions (Tacho's personal writing — the most sophisticated position in the corpus).** Team/system metrics are legitimate for individuals **when influencing that system is the person's actual job** (staff+/management, DevEx/CI-platform roles); task-level metrics are reasonable for juniors and absurd for staff engineers; and activity data is legitimate as a **debugging tool** when outcomes are missed, never as the primary evaluation instrument. "Evidence doesn't have to mean activity data."

4. **Coaching-context (LinearB, Jellyfish, Waydev's marketing).** Individual data exists in the product, positioned for 1:1s rather than ranking. The empirical problem is healsdata's three-employers datapoint — two of three began using it for employment decisions immediately — plus the pricing argument: expensive tools force ROI justification, which pushes buyers toward per-person legibility.

**The strongest single line for the "measurement can be right and still fail" case** is Faros AI, Jan 2026: "**Individual velocity was real. System-level impact was not.**" It is the empirical vindication of Core 4's counterbalancing design and, simultaneously, the reason individual scoring is a category error rather than merely an unfair one.

**The most useful open question to put to DX:** the framework says "never at the individual level," Houck reaffirms it in 2026 even after building TrueThroughput normalization, and yet the product ships a Personal dashboard with PR throughput and review activity, on by default, disabled only by an org-admin toggle. Swarmia made that a product constraint; DX made it a setting. That distinction is defensible — DX's view is the IC's own — but it is exactly where the vendor critique lands, and it is the one place where DX's stated position and shipped artifact can be held apart.

These are just my leftover wait-timers expiring; both research agents had already reported and the full synthesis was delivered in my previous message. No further work is pending.

Summary of what was delivered:

**Thread A (DX Core 4)** — full framework with verbatim definitions and primary/secondary metrics, published benchmarks, the DXI's 13-minutes-per-point ROI claim (with the LeadDev "ten minutes" discrepancy flagged), and the AI Measurement Framework.

The critical finding on individual measurement: your hypothesis is half right, and the wrong half is more interesting. DX's *published* language is an absolute prohibition with no coaching carve-out — "It is critical that this metric is never used at the individual level or tied to performance evaluations." But DX's *product* ships a Personal dashboard with individual PR throughput and review activity, on by default, disabled only via an org-admin toggle. The coaching/outlier carve-out you were looking for lives at **Swarmia** and in **Laura Tacho's personal writing**, not in Core 4.

Highest-value finds: the Kent Beck × Abi Noda interview DX paid for ("if you just sell the dashboard, that's malpractice"); Brian Houck's June 2026 update conceding PR throughput is a poor individual instrument *even after* DX built AI normalization; and Tacho's own account of rolling out GitPrime to 300+ developers at CloudBees — "It was a flop" — which bridges both threads.

**Thread B** — the GitPrime→Flow arc ($170M → equity written to zero → EOL Dec 2027) with verified Hacker News testimony including the `if (false) { // old code }` artifact; the vendor landscape sorted by whether the anti-individual guardrail is architecture (Swarmia) or documentation (Waydev); LinearB's "Core 4 fails the vanity metric test" attack; and the McKinsey backlash with Beck/Orosz, Dan North, Booch, Farley, and Majors.

Corrections worth carrying: Laura Tacho is now at AWS (DX CTO 2023–2026); Beck/Orosz is two parts, not 3–4; Wenjie Wu is not a McKinsey author; Code Climate Velocity killed only its free tier; no Kent Beck writing on GitPrime exists; and the Musk/lines-of-code claim needs independent verification.
